The
Regulating Act, 1773
established the first Supreme Court at Fort William, Calcutta, in 1774.
The Charter Act of 1813 provided for spending at least ₹1 lakh per year on the education of Indians for the first time.
The Charter Act of 1833 made the Governor-General of Bengal the first Governor-General of India.
The Charter Act of 1853 introduced open competition for the Civil Services.
The first meeting of the Constituent Assembly was held on 9 December 1946.
Dr. Rajendra Prasad
became the first permanent elected Chairman/President of the Constituent Assembly on 11 December 1946.
The First Amendment Act of 1951 added the Ninth Schedule.
The parliamentary form of government was first introduced in Great Britain.
The first joint sitting of Parliament was held in 1961.
The Estimates Committee was constituted for the first time in 1950.
Justice M. Fathima Beevi
became the first woman Judge of the Supreme Court in 1989.
The doctrine of Judicial Review was first propounded in the USA.
The Federal Court was inaugurated on 1 October 1937, not in 1950.
Sarojini Naidu
was the first woman Governor of any State, serving in Uttar Pradesh.
Gulzarilal Nanda was the first Deputy Chairman of the Planning Commission.
Sukumar Sen
was the first Chief Election Commissioner, serving from 1950 to 1958.
Rajasthan was the first state to inaugurate Panchayati Raj, while Andhra Pradesh was the second.
Political parties received constitutional recognition for the first time in 1985.
Panchayati Raj was first inaugurated on 2 October 1959 at Nagaur in Rajasthan.
Macaulay was the first Law Member of the Governor-General's Council.

The Indian Councils Act 1909 marked the first association of Indians with both the Viceroy’s and Governors’ Executive Councils, and Satyendra Prasad Sinha became the first Indian Law Member of the Viceroy’s Executive Council.
The Indian Councils Act 1909 was known as the Morley-Minto reforms and introduced separate electorates for Muslims.
The Government of India Act 1919 first made the Central Legislature bicameral, introduced dyarchy in the provinces, and used the term “responsible government.”.
The Act first provided for an All-India Federation, but it never came into existence; it also introduced dyarchy at the Centre, which was never implemented.
The Government of India Act 1935 abolished dyarchy in the provinces and separated Burma from India.
The Government of India Act 1935 created Sindh and Orissa as new provinces.
The Government of India Act 1935 vested residuary powers in
the Governor-General
M.N. Roy first put forward the idea in 1934.

Sinha presided temporarily at the first meeting; Rajendra Prasad was elected permanent President on 11 December 1946; Frank Anthony was the first nominated temporary Deputy Chairman; and H.C. Mukherjee was the first permanent Vice-President.
The Objectives Resolution was moved at the fifth meeting of the first session, and H.C. Mukherjee was the first permanent Vice-President.
B.N. Rau prepared the first draft of the Constitution as Constitutional Advisor.
The Constituent Assembly had 15 women members.
The Interim Government was announced on 24 August 1946.

The Constitution of India Bill of 1895 made the first explicit demand for Fundamental Rights; the First Amendment restricted Article 19 rights, and the First Schedule lists the States and Union Territories.
Pratibha Patil was the first woman President of India.
Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel was the first Deputy Prime Minister, while Indira Gandhi was the first Prime Minister who was a Rajya Sabha member at appointment.
The first Lok Sabha general election was held in 1951–52, and the first session of the First Lok Sabha began on 13 May 1952.
Nargis Dutt was the first actress nominated to the Rajya Sabha, and her nomination took place in 1980.
The Chamber of Princes had 120 members and was created under the Government of India Act 1919.
The Public Accounts Committee was first set up in 1921 under the Government of India Act 1919.
Sucheta Kripalani was the first woman Chief Minister of any State.
President's Rule under Article 356 was first imposed in PEPSU in 1953, according to some sources.
According to another account, the First Finance Commission was set up in 1952, with K.C. Neogy as its first Chairman.
Jawaharlal Nehru was the ex-officio Chairman of the Planning Commission.
The sheet records two accounts: one places the first establishment of the Inter-State Council in May 1990, while another places it in December 1990.
Ombudsman originated in Sweden in 1809; the First Administrative Reforms Commission was established in 1966, recommended Lokpal and Lokayuktas, and had its interim report submitted by Morarji Desai.
The first Lokpal Bill was presented in 1968.
Maharashtra was the first state to introduce the Lokayukta, in 1971 or 1972.
The first Chairman of the National Human Rights Commission assumed office in 1993.
The voting age was lowered to 18 by the 61st Amendment.
VVPAT was first used in the
Noksen Assembly by-election in Nagaland
on 4 September 2013.
The 52nd Amendment provided constitutional recognition to political parties through the Tenth Schedule or anti-defection provisions.
The First Official Language Commission was established in 1955.
Madras had the first Municipal Corporation in India in 1688; Nehru inaugurated Panchayati Raj at Nagaur; and Madhya Pradesh was the first state to implement the 73rd Amendment in its true spirit.
The
Community Development Programme
was the first major rural development programme after independence.
G.V. Mavalankar was the first Speaker of the Lok Sabha and had also been the first Speaker of the Central Legislative Assembly in 1925.
The first Public Interest Litigation considered was Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar in 1979.

Article 1 provides that India is a Union of States.
Article 2 concerns the admission or establishment of new States.
Article 13 provides that laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights are void and is linked with judicial review.
Article 14 deals with equality before law, while Article 17 provides for the abolition of Untouchability.
Article 37 provides that the Directive Principles of State Policy are not enforceable.
Article 39A provides equal justice.
Articles 14, 21 and 32 deal with Fundamental Rights.
Article 21A
provides the Right to Education.
Article 52 concerns the existence of the President; Article 54 the election; Article 60 the oath; and Article 61 the procedure for impeachment.
Article 64 provides that the Vice-President is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.
Article 93 concerns the Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha.
Articles 109–110 deal with the special procedure for Money Bills, and
Article 110
contains the definition of a Money Bill.
Article 124 concerns the establishment and constitution of the Supreme Court.
Article 248 assigns residuary powers to Parliament, while Article 249 permits Parliament to legislate on the State List in the national interest.
Article 356 concerns President’s Rule on failure of constitutional machinery.
Article 280 concerns the Finance Commission.
Articles 243 to 243O
deal with Panchayats under the 73rd Amendment.
Article 12 defines “State”; Article 15 prohibits discrimination; Article 16 provides equality of opportunity in public employment; and Article 18 abolishes titles.

Article 20 concerns protection in respect of conviction; Article 22 concerns arrest and detention; Article 23 prohibits traffic in human beings and forced labour; and Article 24 prohibits the employment of children.
Article 21A was introduced by the 86th Amendment.
Articles 33 to 35 concern modification of Fundamental Rights for forces and other specified groups, while Article 36 defines “State”.
Articles 38 and 39 address social order and principles of policy including livelihood and equal pay under Article 39(d), while Article 39A was inserted by the 42nd Amendment.
Article 41
concerns the right to work.
Article 36 defines “State”; Article 43 concerns living wage; Article 49 concerns protection of monuments; and Article 51 concerns promotion of international peace.
Articles 43A, 48A and 39A were inserted by the 42nd Amendment, while Article 45 originally concerned free education until 14 and now concerns early childhood care.
Article 46 concerns the promotion of the educational interests of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.
Article 47 deals with raising nutrition levels and prohibiting intoxicating drinks, while Article 48 concerns the organisation of agriculture.
Article 40
concerns the organisation of Village Panchayats.
Article 47 directs the State to prohibit intoxicating drinks.
Article 51A contains 11 Fundamental Duties; the duties were added by the 42nd Amendment, while the 11th duty was added by the 86th Amendment.
Article 53 vests the executive power of the Union in the
President
Article 55 concerns the manner of election of the President.
Articles 63, 65, 66 and 67 deal respectively with the existence of the Vice-President, acting as President, election, and the term and removal of the Vice-President.

Article 74 concerns the Council of Ministers aiding and advising the President; Article 75(3) provides collective responsibility; Article 75(1A) concerns the size limit of the Council of Ministers; and Article 76 concerns the Attorney-General.
Article 75 covers other provisions regarding Ministers, Article 75(1A) was inserted by the 91st Amendment, and Article 77 concerns the conduct of the business of the Government of India.
Article 79 concerns the constitution of Parliament.
Article 85 concerns sessions, prorogation and dissolution of Parliament.
Article 100 concerns voting and quorum in Parliament.
Article 116 concerns both Votes on Account and Votes of Credit.
Article 127 concerns ad hoc Judges; Article 129 makes the Supreme Court a Court of Record; Article 131 concerns its original jurisdiction; and Articles 132 to 136 concern its appellate jurisdiction.
Article 141 concerns the binding nature of Supreme Court law; Article 143 concerns advisory jurisdiction through a Presidential reference.
Article 215 makes High Courts Courts of Record, Article 216 concerns their constitution, Article 217 concerns High Court Judges, and Article 233 concerns District Judges.
Articles 245–255 deal with legislative relations; Articles 246, 250, 252 and 253 concern the specified legislative subjects and circumstances.
Articles 256–263 concern administrative relations, and Article 263 concerns the Inter-State Council.
Articles 268–281 concern distribution of revenues, and Article 281 concerns the recommendations of the Finance Commission.
Article 352 concerns a National Emergency proclamation.
Article 354 concerns revenue-distribution provisions during an Emergency; Article 355 imposes the Union’s duty to protect States.
Article 360
concerns a Financial Emergency.
Article 312 concerns All-India Services.

Articles 315–323 concern Public Service Commissions; Article 326 concerns adult suffrage; Articles 330–334 concern reservation of seats for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Anglo-Indians; and Articles 343–351 concern the Official Language.
Article 368 concerns Parliament’s power to amend the Constitution, while Articles 371 to 371J provide special provisions for certain States.
Article 370 concerned temporary provisions for Jammu and Kashmir.
Article 43 concerns living wage, Article 43A was inserted by the 42nd Amendment, Article 44 concerns a Uniform Civil Code, and Article 45 concerns early childhood care.
Article 48 covers animal husbandry and cow protection, Article 49 protects monuments, and Article 50 concerns separation of the judiciary from the executive.
Article 43A concerns the participation of workers in management.
Article 19
contains the six freedoms under Article 19(1)(a) to Article 19(1)(g).

Article 338A concerns the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes; Article 338B concerns the National Commission for Backward Classes; Article 243ZD concerns District Planning Committees; and Article 243ZE concerns Metropolitan Planning Committees.

The parliamentary form of government was borrowed from Britain, DPSP from Ireland, federation with a strong Centre from Canada, and the Concurrent List from Australia.
The procedure established by law was borrowed from Japan.
The Fundamental Duties were borrowed from the USSR.
The idea of the Preamble was borrowed from the USA, not France.
The Government of India Act, 1935 provided the structural and administrative backbone.
The Cabinet system was borrowed from
Britain (UK)
Rule of Law, single citizenship, bicameral legislature, parliamentary privileges and prerogative writs were all borrowed from Britain.
All three provisions—Fundamental Rights, independence of the judiciary and impeachment of the President—were borrowed from the USA.
Ireland was the source for both the method of election of the President and the nomination of members to the Rajya Sabha.
Residuary powers with the Centre, appointment of Governors by the Centre and the advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court were borrowed from Canada.
The joint sitting of both Houses, freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse, and the language of the Preamble were borrowed from Australia.
The ideals of liberty, equality and fraternity in the Preamble were borrowed from France.

The federal scheme, Governor, judiciary, emergency provisions and Public Service Commission were associated with the Government of India Act, 1935, which provided the structural and administrative backbone.

M.N. Roy
proposed the first idea of a Constituent Assembly in 1934.
The Constituent Assembly had 389 planned seats.
The Assembly members were elected by the Provincial Legislative Assemblies, making the election indirect.
Jawaharlal Nehru chaired the Union Constitution Committee.
British India was allotted 296 seats in the Constituent Assembly.
Jawaharlal Nehru moved the Objectives Resolution on 13 December 1946.
Three committees—the Steering Committee, Rules of Procedure Committee and Flag Committee (Ad-hoc)—were chaired by Dr. Rajendra Prasad.
B.N. Rau was the Constitutional Advisor and prepared the first draft with 243 Articles and 13 Schedules.
The Swaraj Party made the first formal demand at the Ranchi Conference in May 1934.
The Cripps Mission made the final proposal for an elected Constituent Assembly in 1942.
The election result was Congress 208 seats, Muslim League 73 seats and other groups 15 seats.
The election used restricted franchise under the Government of India Act, 1935, and the restrictions were based on tax, education and property qualifications.
The Princely States initially stayed away from the Assembly and began joining from its third session in April 1947.
The first meeting was held on 9 December 1946.

The Constitution was adopted on the last day of the eleventh session; the final signing meeting was on 24 January 1950, it came into force on 26 January 1950, and the Assembly took 2 years, 11 months and 17 days to complete its work.
The Constituent Assembly held 11 sessions over 165 sitting days, and its final meeting was held on 24 January 1950.
Dr. Rajendra Prasad was both the Permanent President and Chairman.
Dr. B.R. Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee, which had six other members besides its Chairman.
Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar was an other member of the Drafting Committee.
N. Madhava Rao later replaced B.L. Mitter on the Drafting Committee.

Sardar Patel chaired the Provincial Constitution Committee; H.C. Mukherjee chaired the Minorities Sub-Committee; Jawaharlal Nehru chaired the States Committee; and K.M. Munshi chaired the Order of Business Committee.

The Constitution originally had 8 Schedules and presently has 12 Schedules.
The 9th Schedule was added by the 1st Constitutional Amendment in 1951.
The 9th Schedule was introduced by the 1st Amendment in 1951 to validate certain Acts and Regulations, mainly land reform laws, and protect them from judicial review.
The 1st Schedule contains the names of the States and Union Territories.
Konkani, Manipuri and Nepali were added by the 71st Amendment in 1992, not by the 92nd Amendment.

The Second Schedule deals with emoluments, allowances and privileges; the Third with oaths and affirmations; the Fifth with Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes; and the Sixth with tribal areas in the four specified States.
The First, Second, Third and Fourth Schedules were all part of the original Constitution.
The
Seventh Schedule
was part of the original Constitution and deals with the division of powers through the Union, State and Concurrent Lists.
The Tenth Schedule provides for disqualification of MPs and MLAs.
The Union List originally contained 97 subjects.
The Ninth Schedule originally contained 13 Acts and now contains around 284 Acts.
The Anti-Defection Law, associated with the Tenth Schedule, was amended further by the
91st Amendment

Part XIV-A
deals with Tribunals and covers Articles 323-A to 323-B.
Part XVIII deals with Emergency Provisions.
Part IX deals with the Panchayats, and its inclusion is noted as having been made through the 73rd Amendment, 1992.

Part I covers Articles 1 to 4; Part II covers Articles 5 to 11; Part IV deals with the Directive Principles of State Policy and covers Articles 36 to 51; and Part VIII covers Articles 239 to 242 and deals with the Union Territories.
Part IV-A was added by the 42nd Amendment of 1976.
Part V deals with the Union, including the Executive, Parliament and Judiciary.

Part XVI covers Articles 330–342 and was original.
Parts XX, XXI and XXII were original; Part XXII covers the Short Title, Commencement, Authoritative Text in Hindi and Repeals.

the Co-operative Societies

Article 74 provides for the Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister at the head to aid and advise the President.
The Prime Minister is the real executive head of the Union.
The President is the nominal and constitutional head of the Union.
The oath of the Prime Minister is administered by the President.
The Prime Minister is the Chairman of NITI Aayog, the National Development Council, the National Integration Council and the Inter-State Council.
Article 74 concerns aid and advice, Article 75 concerns Ministers, Article 78 concerns the Prime Minister’s duties, and Article 75(3) concerns collective responsibility.
The 15% limit, applicable to the Union and the States, was introduced by the 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003, and is referred to in Article 75(1A).
Collective responsibility to the Lok Sabha means that the Council of Ministers, including the Prime Minister, must resign when a No-Confidence Motion is passed.
The Prime Minister is the leader of the majority party or coalition in the Lok Sabha and is normally the leader of the majority party there.
A person may be appointed without being an MP, but must become a member of Parliament within six months under Article 75(5).
The Prime Minister allocates portfolios to Ministers.
The Prime Minister communicates all decisions of the Council of Ministers to the President.
The Prime Minister is described as the leader of the Lok Sabha, the Leader of the House and the chief spokesperson of the Government.
The Planning Commission was the earlier body chaired by the Prime Minister before NITI Aayog.
The Prime Minister advises the President on the appointment of other Ministers.
Jawaharlal Nehru is identified as both the first Prime Minister of India and the longest-serving Prime Minister of India.
Indira Gandhi was the first woman Prime Minister of India and was initially a Rajya Sabha member as Prime Minister.
The Deputy Prime Minister is not a constitutional post; it is only a political post.

Article 52 provides that there shall be a President of India.
The President is elected indirectly.
The President is the constitutional head, while the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister constitutes the real executive.
These correspond respectively to Articles 52, 53, 72 and 123.
Nominated members of Parliament do not participate in the Presidential election.
The President addresses the resignation to the
Vice-President
In case of the President’s death, resignation, removal or other vacancy, the Vice-President acts as President under Article 65.
Elected members of State Legislative Assemblies do not participate in the impeachment of the President.
The President may seek a non-binding advisory opinion under Article 143 and may return a Bill only once, except a Money Bill.
Dr. Rajendra Prasad was the first President of India.
Three Articles—352, 356 and 360—relate to National Emergency, President’s Rule and Financial Emergency respectively.
The President promulgates Ordinances when
Parliament is not in session
The President exercises the Union’s executive power directly or through subordinate officers and is described as the First Citizen and a symbol of the nation’s unity, integrity and solidarity.
Article 53(2) identifies the President as the
Supreme Commander of the Defence Forces
Elected members of both Houses of Parliament and elected members of State Legislative Assemblies form part of the Electoral College.
The value of an MLA’s vote is calculated to ensure uniformity among the states.
A presidential candidate must be a citizen of India, at least 35 years old, qualified for election to the Lok Sabha and must not hold an office of profit.
Article 57 permits the President to be re-elected any number of times.
Impeachment for violation of the Constitution is dealt with under Article 61; either House may prefer the charge, and a special majority is required in both Houses.
The President’s Succession Act
deals with succession when both the offices of President and Vice-President are vacant.
The President appoints the Prime Minister, other Ministers, Governors and Judges of the Supreme Court.
The President appoints Judges of the High Courts, the CAG, the Attorney General, the UPSC Chairman and members, Election Commissioners, and members of the Finance Commission.
The President normally appoints the leader of the majority party as Prime Minister.
The President is an integral part of Parliament, summons and prorogues it, dissolves the Lok Sabha, addresses Parliament under Article 87, and assents to Bills under Article 111.
The President has an absolute veto.
The President nominates 12 members to the Rajya Sabha.
The President has the power to grant reprieves under Article 72.
The President holds office for five years under
Article 56
The President declares war and concludes peace on the advice of the Council of Ministers, and appoints Ambassadors and High Commissioners.
The President may dismiss a government that has lost its majority.
The President may return the advice of the Council of Ministers once for reconsideration, and this power was provided by the 44th Amendment.
Pratibha Patil was the 12th President by the stated tenure count.
The President holds Rank 1 in the Order of Precedence.

Article 63 provides that there shall be a Vice-President of India.
The Vice-President is elected by members of both Houses of Parliament, including elected and nominated members.
The Vice-President can be removed by a resolution of the Rajya Sabha.
Article 64 specifically provides that the Vice-President is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.
The term of office of the Vice-President is five years under Article 67.
State Legislative Assemblies do not participate in the Vice-Presidential election.
The Vice-President resigns by addressing the President, and the oath is administered by the President.
The Vice-President must be qualified for election as a Rajya Sabha member, not a Lok Sabha member.
The Vice-President may act as President for a maximum period of
six months
, within which the election for a new President must be held.
The Vice-President is the second-highest constitutional office after the President, and the office is modelled on the American Vice-President.
Article 71 provides that the Supreme Court decides all doubts and disputes regarding the Vice-Presidential election.

The Vice-President may be re-elected any number of times and, as Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, presides over its sittings, exercises a casting vote in a tie, and does not preside during consideration of a resolution for his removal.
The office of the President can fall vacant due to death.
As Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, the Vice-President draws salary and allowances, which are not charged on the Consolidated Fund of India in the capacity of Vice-President.

The Presidential Electoral College includes Members of Parliament and Members of the Legislative Assemblies of States and Union Territories; the President’s qualification is linked to Lok Sabha eligibility; and removal is by impeachment by both Houses of Parliament.
The President is an integral part of Parliament, whereas the Vice-President is not a part of Parliament.
The President addresses the resignation to
the Vice-President
Dr. S. Radhakrishnan was the longest-serving Vice-President and served two terms.
The Vice-President is not a member of either House of Parliament.
